statement_record.book: Display (7.73) exhibits a sentence of the formal internal language of a topos, ∀(t : T). ∃(s : S). f(s) = t. The surrounding prose separates the LOGICAL side (expressions built by strict formal rules; proofs are deductions) from the SEMANTIC side (facts about the sheaves themselves), defines providing SEMANTICS to be giving a compiler that turns each formal statement into a mathematical statement about the objects of the topos, calls the semantics SOUND when every formal proof compiles to a true fact, and asserts that EVERY topos carries such an internal language with a sound semantics — categorical, a.k.a. Kripke-Joyal, semantics.

statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker, and weaker at exactly the layer the display lives in. THE APPARATUS IS PRESENT, THE LOGIC IS NOT. (a) A formal LANGUAGE of types and terms exists — Instance/AST.v's Obj/Hom (the free bicartesian closed syntax) and Instance/Lambda/Exp.v's de Bruijn STLC — and [interp] is precisely the book's 'compiler': it turns each piece of syntax into a mathematical statement in ANY bicartesian closed model, so the 'every ... carries such a semantics' shape is realized parametrically, but over CCC/BCCC models, not over toposes. (b) A formal language of STATEMENTS with the propositional connectives exists — Solver/Expr.v's [Expr] with Top, Bottom, And, Or, Impl and an atomic Equiv of two arrow terms — with [exprD] compiling each formal statement into a genuine mathematical statement about arrows (f ≈ g and its Coq-level ∧, +, →), and [expr_sound]/[exprAD_sound]/[expr_tauto] give exactly 'a verified formal derivation compiles to a true fact'. (c) WHAT IS MISSING is the whole first-order/higher-order layer that display (7.73) uses: there is no quantifier of any kind in either in-tree language (no ∀, no ∃, hence sentence (7.73) is not even expressible), no Ω-valued formula, no equality predicate as a subobject, no forcing relation and no Kripke-Joyal clauses, and the interpreting categories are CCC/BCCC rather than toposes. In-tree soundness is also a narrower notion than the book's: [expr_sound]/Instance/Lambda/Sound.v's [soundness] ('reduction preserves denotation') are soundness for an EQUATIONAL theory of arrows, not for a deductive calculus over logical formulas.

gap: The display's sentence itself is not expressible in-tree: neither formal language has quantifiers (Solver/Expr.v's Expr is purely propositional over arrow equations; Instance/AST.v's Hom and Instance/Lambda's Exp are quantifier-free typed terms with no proposition type), there is no Ω-valued formula layer, and Ω never appears in either syntax. Missing pieces, precisely: (1) a formal internal language whose types are objects and whose formulas are terms of type Ω, with ∀/∃ interpreted by right/left adjoints to base change — the library has no base-change functor f^* and no LCCC structure at all (grep 'pullback functor|base change|locally cartesian' finds only Theory/Morphisms/Stability.v's pullback-pasting lemmas and prose); (2) the Kripke-Joyal forcing relation U ⊩ φ and its clauses; (3) a soundness theorem for a deductive calculus (the in-tree soundness results are for reduction/decision procedures over arrow equations); (4) the interpretation is into a bicartesian closed category, never into a topos — the only ElementaryTopos witness in the tree is FinSet_Topos (Instance/FinSet/Topos.v:38) and no interpretation targets it. The Mitchell-Benabou language and Lawvere-Tierney topologies appear in-tree ONLY as prose in Structure/Topos.v:84-90.

CALIBRATION CAVEAT, recorded rather than overturned: only the Instance/AST.v `interp` leg legitimately supports PARTIAL — it is Lambek's internal language of a (bi)cartesian closed category, i.e. the equational fragment on which the Mitchell-Benabou language is built. The Solver/* leg is weaker than the record's framing suggests: Solver/Expr.v's `Expr` is a REFLECTION TACTIC's goal syntax and `exprD` compiles it into EXTERNAL Coq propositions about morphism equality, not into subobjects/Omega-valued truth of any topos, so 'the formula-to-fact compiler' is an analogy, not an instance of Kripke-Joyal semantics. A strict reading of the frozen PARTIAL definition ('some of the ITEM exists') would give ABSENT, since the display's sentence is, as the record itself states, not expressible in-tree. PARTIAL is kept because the record's strength_comparison and gap are explicit and honest about exactly this ('THE APPARATUS IS PRESENT, THE LOGIC IS NOT'; 'sentence (7.73) is not even expressible'), and the CCC internal language is a genuine sub-layer of the item's claim.

statement_record.book: For any set A there is a sheaf on the interval domain assigning to EVERY open U the same set A, with identity restriction maps; it is called the constant sheaf on A. It lets integers, reals or letters of an alphabet be read as behavior types: an element of A is a behavior that never changes over any interval (7 is the behavior that is always 7).
statement_record.intree: Program Instance Diagonal {C : Category} (J : Category) : C ⟶ [J, C] := { fobj := fun x => {| fobj := fun _ => x ; fmap := fun _ _ _ => id[x] |}; fmap := fun _ _ f => {| transform := fun _ => f |} }.
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker: the PRESHEAF is present and is in fact exactly the book's object, the SHEAF claim is absent. Instantiating Diagonal at C := Sets and J := the site (a presheaf on a category U being U^op ⟶ Sets, Theory/Sheaf.v:124) gives Δ[J](A) : J ⟶ Sets with fobj _ = A and fmap _ _ _ = id[A] — value A on every open, identity restriction maps, exactly as the book describes; the in-tree version is even slightly stronger on the functorial side, since Diagonal is asserted as a FUNCTOR C ⟶ [J, C], so A ↦ Δ(A) is functorial in A, which the book does not state. What is entirely missing is (i) the site/space (there is no interval domain and no Site instance in-tree, so 'sheaf on the interval domain' is not statable) and (ii) any proof or statement that this presheaf satisfies the sheaf condition — no presheaf whatsoever is proved to be a Sheaf anywhere in the tree.

gap: Only the presheaf half exists, and it exists generically rather than over the space the example names. Missing: (1) the interval domain as a topological space and its site of opens — absent (see def-interval-domain); (2) any instance of Theory/Sheaf.v's Site class (there is none in the tree), hence no way to state 'is a sheaf'; (3) a proof that the constant presheaf satisfies the gluing condition — the library contains no verified sheaf example at all. NOTE FOR A FORMALIZER, since it affects what should be proved: the constant presheaf is NOT a sheaf under the book's own Definition 7.35 when |A| ≥ 2, because the empty family covers ∅ and its (vacuously matching) empty family must glue to a UNIQUE element of P(∅) = A — this is precisely the book's own Example 7.36 (P(∅) ≅ 1). The object that is a sheaf is the sheafification, i.e. the locally-constant-functions sheaf, or the constant presheaf restricted to nonempty opens. Any in-tree statement should target that, not the literal reading of Example 7.78.
